mainTopic: The hole size that ends an earthenware vessel's status as a vessel (and so its ability to become impure), the close of פרק המצניע, and the opening משנה of פרק הזורק on throwing between domains on שבת
overview: This amud finishes the discussion from פרק המצניע about how big a hole must be before a broken כלי חרס stops being a vessel and can no longer become impure. First the גמרא settles a contradiction: large vessels follow one measure, and small vessels follow another. רב אסי then teaches that a regular vessel needs a hole that lets liquid flow in. The tiny 'seeping out' hole is enough only for a shard, because, as מר זוטרא explains, no one patches a shard with another shard. עולא reports two opposite views from ארץ ישראל: the hole must fit a pomegranate, or only a small root. רבי אליעזר gives a middle measure, olives. מר קשישא adds two points in רבי אליעזר's name. Such a vessel is fully pure, like stone vessels. For צמיד פתיל, it keeps working until most of it is broken. After the הדרן, פרק הזורק opens with a משנה. Throwing between a רשות היחיד and a רשות הרבים makes one liable. Throwing from one רשות היחיד to another across a רשות הרבים is a dispute between רבי עקיבא and חכמים. The משנה then compares balconies facing each other with balconies on one level. When the balconies are on one level, passing an object between them is liable but throwing it is not, because the לויים in the משכן handed beams between wagons and never threw them.

steps.title: Big vessels versus small vessels
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא resolves a contradiction about when a broken כלי חרס stops being a vessel. One source applies to large vessels and the other to small vessels.
steps.simpleTranslation: This one (the pomegranate-size hole) is about large vessels, and that one (until most of it is broken) is about small vessels.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers a contradiction raised on the previous amud. It says the two sources are not arguing; each one is talking about a different size of vessel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One source says a pomegranate-size hole ends the vessel's status. Another says the vessel stays a vessel until most of it is broken. The answer: a large vessel stops being a vessel once it has a pomegranate-size hole, while a small vessel, where a pomegranate-size hole might not even be possible, stops only when most of it is broken.

keyTerms.meaning: This one ... and that one; the standard way to split two sources into two different cases

steps.confusionAlert: The question this line answers comes earlier. Do not look for the קשיא here; it already appeared before this line.

phrases.english: This one is about large vessels,
phrases.notes: This one means the measure of a hole the size of a pomegranate.

phrases.english: and that one is about small vessels.
phrases.notes: This one means the measure of 'until most of it is broken.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised on the previous amud between two measures for a broken כלי חרס: a pomegranate-size hole versus most of the vessel being broken
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא by vessel size)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two sources seem to give conflicting measures for the same vessel.
steps.terutzMaskana: Each measure applies to a different size of vessel, so there is no conflict.

steps.title: The standard measure is a hole that lets liquid in
steps.stepSummary: רב אסי teaches that for a כלי חרס the measure is a hole that lets liquid in. The smaller 'seeps out' measure applies only to a broken shard.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אסי said: We learn that for an earthenware vessel, the measure is a hole that lets liquid flow in. The rabbis only said 'a hole that lets liquid seep out' about a shard.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אסי gives a new rule for how big a hole must be before a כלי חרס stops being a vessel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two hole sizes. A tiny hole that lets liquid seep out (מוציא משקה) is not enough for a regular vessel. It needs a bigger hole, one that lets liquid flow in (כונס משקה). The tiny measure is limited to a גיסטרא, a broken shard being used as a container.

keyTerms.meaning: We learn; this is the accepted teaching
A hole big enough for liquid to flow in
A tiny hole through which liquid only seeps out
A broken shard of pottery that is used as a container

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two measures. 'Seeping out' is the smaller hole, and it is enough only for a shard. A regular vessel needs the bigger 'flowing in' hole.

phrases.english: Rav Asi said: They teach:
An earthenware vessel, its measure is a hole that lets liquid in.
And they did not say 'lets liquid seep out'
except regarding a shard alone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from large and small vessels to a different distinction: the type of hole, and regular vessel versus shard
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A regular כלי חרס needs a hole of כונס משקה. Only a גיסטרא loses its status with a hole of מוציא משקה.

steps.title: Why is a shard different?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why a shard loses its status with the smaller hole.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רב אסי's special rule for a shard. This sets up the next step, which gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a regular vessel needs the bigger hole, why does a shard need only the tiny one? The גמרא wants the logic behind the difference.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind רב אסי's rule
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why a גיסטרא loses vessel status with only a seeping hole

steps.title: No one patches a shard with another shard
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא explains that a leaking shard is simply thrown away, so even a tiny hole ends its usefulness.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא, son of רב נחמן, said: Because people do not say, 'Bring a shard to fix a shard.'
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא answers the question. Once a shard leaks, people throw it out instead of fixing it, so it stops being a useful vessel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A shard is already a leftover piece. When it starts to leak, no one bothers to patch it with another shard; they discard it. A regular vessel still has value, so people keep using it until the hole is bigger.
steps.whatToRemember: A regular כלי חרס needs a hole of כונס משקה to stop being a vessel. A גיסטרא needs only מוציא משקה, because people throw away a leaking shard instead of fixing it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a general principle. Whether something counts as a vessel depends on how people actually treat it: a vessel that no one would bother to keep or repair stops being a vessel.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר מָר זוּטְרָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן:
phrases.english: Mar Zutra son of Rav Nachman said:
Because people do not say:
'Bring a shard for a shard.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר זוּטְרָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A leaking shard is not repaired but thrown away, so a small seeping hole already ends its use.

steps.title: A dispute in ארץ ישראל: pomegranate or small root
steps.stepSummary: עולא reports two אמוראים who disagree about the hole size. One says a pomegranate, the other a small root.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said: Two אמוראים in the West disagree about this, רבי יוסי son of רבי אבין and רבי יוסי בר זבדא. One said the hole must fit a pomegranate, and one said the size of a small root.
steps.whatsHappening: עולא brings a new opinion from ארץ ישראל. Two scholars disagree about how big the hole must be for a כלי חרס to stop being a vessel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two views are far apart. One requires a big hole, the size of a pomegranate. The other requires only a tiny hole, the size of a small root.

keyTerms.meaning: One said ... and one said; the formula for a dispute where we are not told who said which

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא does not tell us which רבי יוסי said which opinion. The memory aid in the next step stresses that the two views are the two extremes, one large and one small, and that neither holds the middle measure of olives.

phrases.english: Ulla said:
Two amoraim in the West disagree about this,
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Avin
and Rabbi Yosei bar Zavda.
One said: big enough for a pomegranate to go out,
and one said: like a small root.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר עוּלָּא: פְּלִיגִי בַּהּ תְּרֵי אָמוֹרָאֵי בְּמַעְרְבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings another set of opinions on the same question of hole size
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is a dispute: either a pomegranate-size hole or a small-root-size hole.

steps.title: A memory aid: one gives more, one gives less
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a memory aid for the dispute: one opinion is large and one is small.
steps.simpleTranslation: And your memory aid: 'Both the one who gives more and the one who gives less.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a memory aid to help us remember the dispute just quoted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase אחד המרבה ואחד הממעיט is borrowed from a well-known saying about offerings. Here it reminds us that one opinion takes a large measure (pomegranate) and the other a small measure (root). Some explain that it also tells us that neither of them holds the middle measure, olives, which comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: The one who gives more (makes the measure large)
The one who gives less (makes the measure small)

phrases.english: And your memory aid:
both the one who gives more and the one who gives less.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a memory device for the dispute in step 5
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The two opinions are the large measure and the small measure, not the middle one.

steps.title: A middle measure: the size of olives
steps.stepSummary: רב חיננא בר כהנא, in the name of רבי אליעזר, says the hole must let olives fall out.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חיננא בר כהנא said in the name of רבי אליעזר: An earthenware vessel's measure is a hole that lets olives fall out.
steps.whatsHappening: A third opinion is added. The hole must be big enough for olives to fall through.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a middle position. It is bigger than a small root but smaller than a pomegranate. It fits the memory aid, which said the earlier two scholars took the extremes.

phrases.english: Rav Chinnana bar Kahana said
in the name of Rabbi Eliezer:
An earthenware vessel, its measure is a hole that lets olives out.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִינָּנָא בַּר כָּהֲנָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a middle opinion between the two extremes of step 5
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A כלי חרס stops being a vessel with a hole that lets olives fall out.

steps.title: The holed vessel is fully pure, but צמיד פתיל lasts longer
steps.stepSummary: מר קשישא completes רבי אליעזר's teaching. Once the vessel has this hole, it cannot become impure at all, like dung, stone and earth vessels. For צמיד פתיל, though, it still works until most of it is broken.
steps.simpleTranslation: And מר קשישא, son of רבה, ends it in the name of רבי אליעזר: Such vessels are like dung vessels, stone vessels and earth vessels, which do not become impure, neither by Torah law nor by rabbinic law. But for צמיד פתיל, the vessel keeps working until most of it is broken.
steps.whatsHappening: מר קשישא adds the end of רבי אליעזר's statement. It explains how pure the holed vessel is and gives one exception.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With an olive-size hole, the vessel is completely out of the system of טומאה, with no rabbinic impurity either. It is treated like vessels that never receive טומאה. The exception is צמיד פתיל: a sealed vessel in a tent with a dead body protects its contents. For this purpose, a hole does not cancel the vessel; it keeps protecting until most of it is broken.

keyTerms.meaning: He finishes the statement (adds its ending)
A tightly sealed cover; a sealed vessel in a tent with a corpse protects what is inside

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the vessel becomes 'not a vessel' for every purpose. The olive-size hole ends its ability to receive טומאה, but for צמיד פתיל it keeps working until most of it is broken.
steps.whatToRemember: Hole sizes for a כלי חרס: pomegranate, small root, or olives (רבי אליעזר). With that hole it is fully pure, like stone vessels. For צמיד פתיל, the measure is until most of it is broken.
steps.whyThisMatters: The same vessel can be judged by different standards for different laws. Receiving טומאה and protecting with צמיד פתיל each have their own measure.

phrases.english: And Mar Kashisha son of Rabba
concludes it in the name of Rabbi Eliezer:
And they are like dung vessels
and stone vessels and earth vessels,
which do not receive impurity,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה וְלֹא מִדִּבְרֵי סוֹפְרִים.
phrases.english: neither by Torah law nor by rabbinic law.
And regarding a sealed cover,
only once most of it is broken.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמָר קַשִּׁישָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבָּה מְסַיֵּים בַּהּ מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the statement of רבי אליעזר from step 7
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A holed כלי חרס receives no טומאה at all, but for צמיד פתיל it still works until most of it is broken.

steps.title: הדרן — Closing פרק המצניע
steps.stepSummary: The closing formula for פרק המצניע.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, המצניע.
steps.whatsHappening: This line marks the end of the chapter המצניע. The traditional formula expresses that we will come back to learn it again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No new law is taught here. It simply separates the end of one chapter from the beginning of the next.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you; said at the end of a chapter
Name of the chapter that just ended

phrases.english: We will return to you, HaMatznia

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the chapter that the previous steps concluded
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: פרק המצניע is complete. A new chapter begins.

steps.title: Throwing between domains on שבת
steps.stepSummary: The new chapter's משנה rules that throwing between a רשות היחיד and a רשות הרבים makes one liable. Throwing from one רשות היחיד to another across a רשות הרבים is disputed: רבי עקיבא holds him liable, חכמים exempt him.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One who throws from a private domain to a public domain, or from a public domain to a private domain, is liable. From a private domain to another private domain with a public domain in between: רבי עקיבא holds him liable, and the חכמים exempt him.
steps.whatsHappening: The new chapter begins with a משנה about the מלאכה of moving an object between domains by throwing it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Throwing straight from one type of domain to the other is clearly forbidden, the same as carrying. The new case is an object that starts and ends in private domains but flies over a public domain on the way. רבי עקיבא holds the thrower liable even though the object never landed in the public domain. The חכמים exempt him, since the object only passed through.
steps.confusionAlert: In the dispute, the object never lands in the public domain; it only flies over it. That is exactly why רבי עקיבא and the חכמים disagree.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the major question of the chapter: does an object passing through the air of a domain count as if it rested there? The גמרא will explore this next.

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who throws
from the private domain to the public domain,
or from the public domain to the private domain, is liable.
From the private domain to the private domain
with the public domain in between,
Rabbi Akiva holds him liable,
and the Rabbis exempt him.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַזּוֹרֵק מֵרְשׁוּת הַיָּחִיד לִרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new chapter with a new topic: throwing on שבת
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Throwing between a רשות היחיד and a רשות הרבים makes one liable. Throwing from one רשות היחיד to another across a רשות הרבים is disputed: רבי עקיבא holds him liable, חכמים exempt him.

steps.title: Two balconies facing each other: passing and throwing are both exempt
steps.stepSummary: The משנה gives a concrete case: two balconies face each other across a רשות הרבים. Someone who passes or throws an object from one to the other is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: How so? There are two balconies facing each other across a public domain. Someone who passes an object, or throws it, from one balcony to the other is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה asks "how so?" and gives a real-life picture of carrying between two private areas across a public street. In this first case, the person is פטור whether he hands the object over or throws it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each balcony is a private area, and the street between them is a רשות הרבים. Even though the object crosses over the public street, this setup does not make him liable for either kind of transfer. The next line will give a contrasting case where passing does make him liable.

keyTerms.meaning: Balconies that stick out from buildings
One who passes or hands an object over

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up הַמּוֹשִׁיט and הַזּוֹרֵק. Passing means handing the object across without letting go of it. Throwing means letting it fly through the air. The משנה treats them differently in the next case.

phrases.english: How so?
phrases.notes: Here comes a real-life example of the משנה's rule.

phrases.english: Two balconies facing each other
phrases.notes: Each balcony counts as a private area.

phrases.english: across the public domain,
one who passes or throws from one to the other —
is exempt,

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיצַד? שְׁתֵּי גְזוּזְטְרָאוֹת זוֹ כְּנֶגֶד זוֹ בִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a concrete illustration of the transfer between two private areas across a public street that the משנה introduced in Step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Balconies facing each other across a רשות הרבים: passing and throwing between them are both פטור.

steps.title: Balconies on the same level: passing is liable, throwing is exempt
steps.stepSummary: If both balconies are בדיוטא אחת (on one level), passing an object between them makes one liable, but throwing does not. The reason is that this is how the לויים worked in the משכן.
steps.simpleTranslation: If both balconies were on one level, someone who passes an object between them is liable, but someone who throws it is exempt. This is because that is how the work of the לויים was done.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a second case that splits the two actions. Here passing is חייב and throwing is פטור. The משנה supports this with the words "this was the work of the לויים."
steps.deeperAnalysis: הלכות שבת are learned from the work done in the משכן. Since the לויים did pass things this way, passing counts as a forbidden מלאכה. Throwing was not done this way, so it does not make one liable. The next line explains what that work actually was.

keyTerms.meaning: On one level (or in one row)
The work of the Levites in the משכן

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the basic method of הלכות שבת: an action is a forbidden מלאכה only if it matches how work was done in the משכן.

phrases.english: If both were on one level —
one who passes is liable
and one who throws is exempt,
for this was the work of the Levites.
phrases.notes: The rule comes from how the Levites worked in the משכן.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts with Step 11: changing the position of the balconies makes passing liable.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Balconies בדיוטא אחת: passing is חייב and throwing is פטור, following the work of the לויים.

steps.title: The לויים passed the beams between wagons but did not throw them
steps.stepSummary: The משנה describes the work of the לויים. Two wagons stood one behind the other in a public area, and the לויים passed the beams of the משכן from one wagon to the other but never threw them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Two wagons stood one behind the other in the public domain. They passed the beams from one to the other, but they did not throw them.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now explains exactly what "the work of the לויים" was. This is the source for the rule in Step 12.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wagons were like two private areas with public ground between them, just like the two balconies. The לויים handed the heavy beams across but did not throw them. So passing matches the משכן work and is חייב, while throwing does not match it and is פטור.

keyTerms.meaning: Wagons (that carried the parts of the משכן)
The wooden beams of the משכן

steps.whatToRemember: Two balconies facing each other: both actions are פטור. Two balconies on one level: passing is חייב and throwing is פטור. The reason is that the לויים handed the beams between the wagons but did not throw them.

phrases.english: Two wagons, one behind the other,
in the public domain,
they would pass the beams from one to the other,
but they would not throw them.
phrases.notes: The beams were heavy, so throwing was not part of the משכן work.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁתֵּי עֲגָלוֹת זוֹ אַחַר זוֹ בִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the phrase "this was the work of the לויים" from Step 12 and serves as its source.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that passing between balconies on one level is חייב while throwing is פטור.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The work of the לויים in the משכן: passing beams between wagons standing one behind the other, without throwing.
